The symptoms of myasthenia gravis can worsen with respiratory infections and other exacerbating factors.
Gentamicin infusions can exacerbate myasthenia gravis in a 71-year-old man with myasthenia gravis by interfering with neuromuscular transmission.

In a 71-year-old man with myasthenia gravis who developed poor grip strength and progressive difficulty breathing after 5 days of a urinary tract infection treated with gentamicin, these findings suggest a myasthenic crisis.
In a 71-year-old man with cyanosis, weak shallow respirations, and an oxygen saturation of 86% on room air, these findings indicate respiratory failure.

In a 71-year-old man with myasthenia gravis who developed respiratory failure after gentamicin treatment for a urinary tract infection, the most appropriate next step in management is plasmapheresis for likely myasthenic crisis.

Plasmapheresis, also known as plasma exchange, is a method of removing antibodies from the blood and can be effective in managing myasthenic crisis.

Thymectomy is the surgical removal of the thymus gland and is a treatment option for myasthenia gravis, but thymectomy is not the most appropriate next step in management for this 71-year-old man with myasthenia gravis who presents with progressive difficulty breathing and poor grip strength.
